Title: Rome in World Time, Part 8: Gold to Rust: Commodus and the Crisis of the Third Century (AD 180–284)

Summary: Cassius Dio said that after Marcus Aurelius, Rome went from "a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust." In about a century, the Roman throne was auctioned off, emperors were murdered by their own troops one after another, an emperor was captured by Persia, and the empire split into three before Aurelian pieced it back together. In the same decades, Han China collapsed into the Three Kingdoms, a new Persian dynasty rose, Queen Himiko sent envoys from Japan, and Maya cities entered their Classic age.

---

Between 235 and 284, roughly 26 men were recognised as emperor in Rome, plus dozens of usurpers. Almost all of them died violently. The empire faced invasions on two fronts, plague, a collapsing currency and breakaway states. It survived, but it came out the other side a very different, much more militarised state.

## Commodus (180–192)

Marcus' son **Commodus** made peace on the Danube and came home. He was more interested in fighting as a gladiator in the arena than in governing.

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 182 | His sister **Lucilla** organises an assassination attempt; it fails |
| 185 | 1,500 soldiers from the army in **Britain** march to Rome to accuse the Praetorian Prefect Perennis; Commodus hands him over and he is killed |
| 186–187 | **Maternus**, an army deserter, leads bands of deserters and outlaws through Gaul and Spain in the "War of the Deserters," and reportedly plots to kill Commodus in Rome |
| 189 | A grain shortage leads to a riot against the chamberlain **Cleander**, who is executed |
| 31 Dec 192 | Commodus is strangled in his bath by a wrestler named Narcissus |

## The Year of the Five Emperors and the Severans (193–235)

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| Jan–Mar 193 | **Pertinax** tries to restore discipline; the Praetorians kill him after 87 days |
| Mar 193 | The Praetorians **auction off the empire**. The senator **Didius Julianus** wins with a bid of 25,000 sesterces per soldier |
| 193 | Three armies proclaim their generals: **Septimius Severus** (Danube), **Pescennius Niger** (Syria), **Clodius Albinus** (Britain). Severus takes Rome; Didius is killed |
| 194 | Severus beats Niger at Issus |
| 195–196 | Byzantium holds out for Niger for over two years and is sacked |
| 197 | **Lugdunum** (Lyon): Severus beats Albinus in one of the largest Roman civil-war battles |
| 197–198 | Severus sacks Ctesiphon; makes northern **Mesopotamia** a province |
| 208–211 | Severus campaigns in Scotland; dies at **York** in February 211, telling his sons "Be harmonious, enrich the soldiers, scorn all others" |
| Dec 211 | **Caracalla** has his brother and co-emperor **Geta** murdered in their mother's arms |
| **212** | The **Constitutio Antoniniana** makes nearly every free person in the empire a Roman citizen |
| 213 | First mention of the **Alamanni** on the Rhine |
| 215 | Caracalla massacres young men of **Alexandria** after they mock him |
| 217 | Caracalla is murdered on the way to a temple near Carrhae; his Praetorian Prefect **Macrinus** becomes the first emperor who was not a senator |
| 218 | Legions in Syria revolt for the teenage **Elagabalus**, a priest of the sun god of Emesa; Macrinus is defeated |
| 222 | Praetorians kill Elagabalus and throw his body into the Tiber; his cousin **Severus Alexander** succeeds |
| c. 223–228 | The Praetorians murder the great jurist **Ulpian**, their own prefect |
| **224** | In Persia, **Ardashir** defeats the last Parthian king. The **Sasanian** Empire is born |
| 230–232 | Severus Alexander fights the new Persians to a draw |
| 235 | His soldiers on the Rhine murder him and his mother at Mainz |

## The Crisis of the Third Century (235–284)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 235 | **Maximinus Thrax**, a giant ex-peasant soldier, becomes emperor. He never visits Rome |
| **238** | **Year of the Six Emperors**: landowners in Africa revolt over taxes and proclaim **Gordian I** and his son **Gordian II** (killed within three weeks); the Senate appoints **Pupienus and Balbinus**; Maximinus is murdered by his own troops besieging Aquileia; the Praetorians kill Pupienus and Balbinus; the 13-year-old **Gordian III** survives |
| 238 | **Goths** sack Histria on the Black Sea |
| 244 | Gordian III dies after a defeat by Persia at Misiche. **Philip the Arab** becomes emperor and pays Persia for peace |
| **21 Apr 248** | Rome celebrates its **1,000th birthday** with huge games |
| 248–249 | Rebellions of Pacatianus on the Danube and Jotapianus in the East |
| 249 | **Decius** is proclaimed by his troops and kills Philip |
| 250 | **Decian persecution**: every citizen must sacrifice to the gods and obtain a certificate |
| 250s–260s | **Plague of Cyprian** spreads across the empire |
| **251** | **Abritus**: Decius is killed by the Goths under Cniva, the first emperor to die in battle against a foreign enemy |
| 253 | Persia's **Shapur I** sacks Antioch; **Valerian** becomes emperor |
| 256 | Persia takes **Dura-Europos** on the Euphrates |
| 257–258 | Valerian's persecution; Bishop Cyprian of Carthage is executed |
| **260** | **Edessa**: Valerian is **captured by Shapur**, the only Roman emperor ever taken prisoner. He dies in captivity. His son **Gallienus** rules alone |
| 260 | Usurpers everywhere: Ingenuus and Regalianus on the Danube, Macrianus and Quietus in the East |
| **260–274** | **The Gallic Empire**: **Postumus** sets up a separate Roman state in Gaul, Britain and Spain |
| c. 260 | The **Agri Decumates** (the land between the upper Rhine and Danube) is abandoned |
| 260–267 | **Odaenathus** of Palmyra beats the Persians for Rome, reaching Ctesiphon |
| 267 | The **Heruli** sack **Athens**, Sparta and Corinth by sea |
| 268 | Gallienus is murdered by his own officers while besieging the usurper Aureolus at Milan |
| 268/269 | **Claudius II** beats the Goths at **Naissus**; dies of plague in 270 |
| **270–272** | **Zenobia**, widow of Odaenathus, rules for her son and takes **Egypt** and much of Asia Minor: the **Palmyrene Empire** |
| 271 | The Juthungi invade Italy; Rome builds the **Aurelian Walls**. In Rome the mint workers revolt under Felicissimus; thousands die in street fighting |
| c. 271–275 | **Dacia** is abandoned, the first province given up for good |
| 272 | **Aurelian** beats Zenobia at Immae and Emesa; she is captured and later paraded in Rome |
| 273 | Palmyra revolts again and is sacked |
| **274** | Aurelian accepts the surrender of the Gallic emperor **Tetricus** at Châlons. The empire is reunited. Aurelian is hailed "Restorer of the World" and dedicates a temple to **Sol Invictus** |
| 275 | Aurelian is murdered by officers tricked into thinking they were on his execution list |
| 276–282 | **Probus** fights invaders on the Rhine and Danube; killed by his own soldiers |
| 283 | **Carus** sacks Ctesiphon and dies (struck by lightning, according to one story) |
| 284 | His son Numerian is found dead in his litter. The army chooses **Diocletian** (20 November 284) |

### Why did the empire nearly fall?

- **Two-front war:** the Sasanians were much more aggressive than the Parthians, and Germanic peoples on the Rhine and Danube were forming larger confederations (Alamanni, Franks, Goths).
- **The army as kingmaker:** since 193, soldiers had learned they could make and unmake emperors, and each new emperor had to pay them.
- **Money:** the silver content of the antoninianus coin fell from about 50% to under 5%, and prices rose.
- **Plague:** two pandemics within a century (Antonine and Cyprian).
- **Regional self-help:** the Gallic and Palmyrene empires were not barbarian kingdoms; they were Roman provinces protecting themselves because the centre could not.

## Things you might not have known happened at the same time

**Rome and Han both broke apart, but only one came back.** China's Han dynasty fell into three kingdoms in 220. Rome split into three (Gallic Empire, Palmyrene Empire, central empire) in the 260s. Rome reunified in 274; China reunified in 280. The timing is remarkably close, and both reunifications proved short-lived in different ways.

**The Yellow Turbans and Maternus.** In 184 China faced a religious mass uprising that brought down the dynasty within a generation. Two years later Gaul and Spain had their own "deserters' war." Rome's revolt was far smaller, but both show states struggling to control their countryside.

**Queen Himiko and Rome's millennium.** Japan's first ruler known from written records died, according to the Chinese *Wei Zhi*, around 247/248. Rome was celebrating its 1,000th anniversary in April 248.

**A Roman emperor knelt to a Persian king.** The rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam in Iran show Shapur I on horseback with Valerian kneeling before him and Philip the Arab begging for peace. It is one of the few depictions of Roman emperors made by their enemies.

**Aksum was counted among the great powers.** In the third century, Mani listed Rome, Persia, China and Aksum as the world's great kingdoms. Most people today have never heard of Aksum.

## What comes next

Part 9: Diocletian splits power four ways, Constantine wins at the Milvian Bridge and founds Constantinople, Christianity goes from persecuted to official, and the Goths crush a Roman army at Adrianople. Meanwhile the Gupta Empire rises in India, China's northern cities fall to Xiongnu, and a Teotihuacan general takes over Tikal.

## Sources and notes

- Cassius Dio, *Roman History*, Books 72–80 (to 229; he was a senator and eyewitness).
- Herodian, *History of the Empire after Marcus* (180–238).
- *Historia Augusta*: the main Latin narrative for 235–284, but notoriously unreliable, with invented documents and people.
- Zosimus, *New History*, Book 1; Zonaras' *Epitome*.
- Shapur I's inscription *Res Gestae Divi Saporis* at Naqsh-e Rostam (the Persian side of the story).
- *Wei Zhi* (Records of Wei, part of the *Sanguozhi*), for Himiko.
- Overview: [Crisis of the Third Century (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century), [Gallic Empire (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallic_Empire), [Himiko (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himiko).

**Flags:** The *Historia Augusta* is the main source for much of this period and is partly fiction, so many details (especially quotes and numbers) are uncertain. The exact count of emperors depends on who you count as legitimate. Himiko's death date and the location of Yamatai are debated. The date of Claudius II's victory at Naissus (268 or 269) and the exact date Dacia was abandoned are disputed. The Classic Maya start date of c. 250 is a convention.
